title: Resting heart rate
why: The heart adapts to weightlessness. A resting HR that slowly climbs above your normal is an early sign of fatigue, poor sleep or illness.
steps: Anchor yourself and rest 5 minutes without effort.
Place index and middle fingers on the inner wrist artery.
Count beats for 60 seconds, or read the number from the oximeter or BP monitor.
ifCritical: With chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or fainting, open Emergency mode now.

sources.label: American Heart Association – Target heart rates

title: Blood pressure
why: Fluids redistribute in weightlessness; very high or very low pressure can signal a heart problem, bleeding or dehydration. Low BP and fainting on landing are a NASA cardiovascular risk.
steps: Sit anchored with feet in the foot restraints and rest 5 minutes.
Put the cuff on a bare arm, supported at heart level.
If high, wait 5 minutes and measure again.
ifWatch: Re-measure tomorrow at the same time.
ifCritical: Above 180/120 after re-measuring: notify the flight surgeon now; with chest pain, weakness or severe headache open Emergency mode.

sources.label: American Heart Association – Understanding blood pressure readings

title: Blood oxygen (SpO2)
why: The cabin is a closed, controlled atmosphere. Low oxygen can come from the lungs, the heart or the environment itself (ppO2, CO2).
steps: Use a warm finger without nail polish.
Keep the hand still at heart level.
Wait for the number to stabilise, then record it. Devices can be off by 2–4%.
ifWatch: Re-measure and check cabin air readings.
ifCritical: ≤ 92: notify flight surgeon and check cabin ppO2/ppCO2. ≤ 88, blue lips/nails or confusion: Emergency mode.

title: Blood glucose
why: Different food, activity and sleep during the mission affect blood sugar; a low can cause dizziness or fainting during hazardous work.
steps: Choose the context: fasting (8 h+), 2 h after a meal, or random.
Clean the finger with an alcohol wipe and let it dry.
Prick the side of the fingertip. In microgravity the drop will not fall; bring the strip to it.
Wipe with gauze and put the lancet in the sharps container.
ifWatch: Re-measure in the same context tomorrow.
ifCritical: < 70: 15/15 rule (15 g fast carbs, re-check in 15 min); if unable to self-treat it is an emergency. ≥ 200: re-measure and notify the flight surgeon.

title: Body temperature
why: Immunity changes in space and infections spread fast in a closed cabin. Your normal in space is about 1 °C higher than on Earth, so your personal baseline matters.
steps: No food, drink or exercise for the last 15 minutes.
Digital thermometer under the tongue, mouth closed until it beeps.
ifWatch: Rest, fluids, re-measure in 4 hours and limit crew contact.
ifCritical: ≥ 39.4 °C or fever over 48–72 h: notify flight surgeon. Confusion, breathing trouble, seizure or severe headache with stiff neck: Emergency mode.

sources.label: Stahn et al. 2017, Scientific Reports – Increased core body temperature in astronauts
